metadata.title: Lecture 6.5 - RMSProp: Divide the Gradient by a Running Average of its Recent Magnitude (Tieleman & Hinton, 2012)
metadata.venue: Coursera Neural Networks for Machine Learning, Lecture 6.5
metadata.framework: Adaptive learning rate method using running average of squared gradients to normalize per-parameter updates
metadata.source_note: Extraction based on well-known content of Tieleman & Hinton (2012 Coursera lecture). No formal paper.

nodes.name: RMSProp update rule
nodes.statement: Maintain a running average of squared gradients: $v_t = \rho \cdot v_{t-1} + (1 - \rho) \cdot g_t^2$ where $g_t = \nabla_\theta L(\theta_t)$ and $\rho$ is the decay rate (typically 0.9). Update parameters: $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{v_t} + \epsilon} \cdot g_t$ where $\eta$ is the learning rate and $\epsilon$ is a small constant for numerical stability.

nodes.name: Per-parameter adaptive learning rate
nodes.statement: Each parameter has its own effective learning rate $\eta / (\sqrt{v_t} + \epsilon)$. Parameters with consistently large gradients get smaller effective learning rates; parameters with small gradients get larger rates. This adapts to the geometry of the loss surface.

nodes.name: Motivation from rprop and Adagrad
nodes.statement: RMSProp is motivated as a mini-batch version of rprop. It can also be viewed as a modification of Adagrad that replaces the accumulation of all past squared gradients (which causes the learning rate to shrink to zero) with an exponential moving average, keeping the learning rate from vanishing.

nodes.name: No first moment (momentum) term
nodes.statement: RMSProp only tracks the second moment (squared gradients). There is no explicit momentum term (first moment estimation). This is the key difference from Adam, which adds bias-corrected first-moment estimation.
